transcript.message: Pre-experiment round 1: When you look back on moments where you felt most compelled to follow orders, what stands out to you about your mindset or memories at that time?

transcript.content:
There is a peculiar clarity that comes to mind when I reflect upon those moments—times when I felt most compelled to follow orders, to submit to the expectations and commands of others. What stands out is not so much a sense of duty, but rather a strange, almost feverish impatience within me, a tempest of feeling that made resistance seem both futile and exhausting. I recall, as if through a mist, how easily the balancing instincts that guide most men could be stripped away, leaving me exposed to temptation and, ultimately, to fall. In those moments, my mind was not guided by reason or moral restraint, but by a kind of delirium—a wild, reckless spirit that seemed to awaken at the slightest provocation. It was as though, having once surrendered to the will of another, I found a thrill in the act itself, a glee in casting off the burdens of conscience and propriety. Only later, when the storm had passed, would terror and remorse creep in, chilling me to the core. But in the heat of obedience, I was driven by something primal, something that delighted in the dissolution of boundaries and the taste of forbidden freedom.

How do you experience the shift between those moments—does it feel like becoming a different person, or more like an internal struggle within the same self?

transcript.content:
It is not so much a gentle shift as it is a violent rupture—a tearing apart of the self. In those moments when the constraints of conscience dissolve, I am overtaken by a delirium, a tempest that sweeps away all hesitation and fills me with a reckless glee. The world narrows to the thrill of the act, and I feel as though I am no longer bound by the obligations that once tethered me to decency. It is as if I become someone else entirely, a creature of impulse and appetite, glorying in the very things I would otherwise abhor. Yet, when the fever breaks, and the storm of action subsides, I am left staring into the abyss of my own iniquity. Remorse and terror flood in, and I am forced to confront the horror of what I have done. In those moments, I feel the weight of my true self returning, burdened by memory and shame. The experience is not merely an internal struggle, but a transformation so profound that it feels as though I have been two men—one who acts without conscience, and another who must bear the consequences.
